{"id": "103:2/q01", "question": "What is the grammatical answer to the oath?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "103:2/q01/p1", "position": "The declaration that humanity is in loss answers the oath by time.", "reasons": "Jishumi identifies the oath wāw and this clause as its answer; Ibn al-Jawzi reports al-Zajjaj; Study Quran takes verses 2–3 as the answer and compares 95:5–6; Corpus Coranicum describes an opening oath followed by rebuke. {"id": "103:2/q02", "question": "Whom does al-insān designate?", "turns_on": "Whether the definite singular is generic, as the following exception suggests, or points to a particular unbeliever or occasion.", "positions": [{"id": "103:2/q02/p1", "position": "Humanity as a whole, with believers subsequently excepted.", "reasons": "Kaʿb includes Adam and his descendants; Abu Ubayda and al-Zajjaj call it a generic noun. Alusi says named losers are examples, not exclusive. Study Quran allows a historical emphasis on humanity's final phase; Elmalili especially includes the last era. Al-Zarkashi and al-Suyuti say the definite singular means every human; the following exception establishes its collective scope. Al-Zarkashi adds that replacing the generic article with 'all' preserves the sense. Ibn Ashur cites the explicit believer exception as a case of the Qur'an qualifying a broad proposition precisely. Ibn ʿĀshūr applies the comprehensive generic to people living when Islam appeared, especially those its call reached worldwide; the believer exception leaves the judgment true of others. Qurtubi calls the generic reading sound on account of the exception."}, {"id": "103:2/q02/p2", "position": "Disbelievers, whose exclusion is made clear by the next verse.", "reasons": "Wahidi reports Muqatil's reading of the unbeliever astray until death; the exception is Bagawi's reason to limit the term. Wahidi specifies one working outside God's obedience and forfeiting a place in Paradise. Ibn Abbas is transmitted by Abu Salih. {"id": "103:2/q03", "question": "How can singular al-insān be followed by an exception for many believers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "103:2/q03/p1", "position": "A singular generic noun denotes the human collective.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda's Majaz compares 70:19–22, 69:47 and a line of al-Nabigha; Tabari reports the same construction elsewhere. Qurtubi compares generic al-nafs and its exceptions in a legal verse. Abu Hayyan and Samin infer generic scope from the exception. Al-Zarkashi and al-Suyuti explicitly infer collective reference from the believer exception; al-Zarkashi adds al-Hajjaj's sermon in which each hearer was addressed as 'O human,' and distinguishes a mentally conceived genus from its external instances (Ibn Babshadh). Their surrounding grammatical surveys distinguish generic al from relative and anaphoric uses, universal individuals from a class's qualities or essence, and definite nouns from other general forms such as kull, relative and conditional words, and possessive or contextually general indefinites. Al-Zarkashi also reports debates about definite plurals and genus versus species. Al-Suyuti calls the following exception specification of the general statement, not abrogation, and gives other form-for-referent substitutions. Ibn Ashur cites this exception as precise qualification. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the generic definite customarily comprehensive, qualified by the believer exception."}, {"id": "103:2/q03/p2", "position": "A definite singular with al does not itself carry universal force.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi reports Fakhr al-Din al-Razi and his followers denying that a singular noun made definite by alif-lam is general. Al-Zarkashi rejects this denial on the strength of the exception in 103:3; his reply says the thief wording in 5:38 instead denotes the essence of theft, reaching every thief across time."}]}
{"id": "103:2/q04", "question": "What wording and vowel readings of this verse are transmitted?", "turns_on": "Which transmitted wording or vocalization is used, and whether an explanatory addition belongs to canonical recitation.", "positions": [{"id": "103:2/q04/p1", "position": "The received codex reads the present wording, with a still sīn in khusr.", "reasons": "Thalabi prefers the general reciters and codices; Qurtubi says Ali's explanatory addition is not Qur'an for recitation under the Uthmanic codex. Jishumi, Abu Hayyan and Samin attest the still sīn as the majority form. Qurtubi explicitly prefers the community's codices and says wording opposed to the Uthmanic codex is not Qur'an for recitation."}, {"id": "103:2/q04/p2", "position": "Khusr is pronounced with ḍamma on the sīn.", "reasons": "Reported from al-Aʿraj, Asim, Talha, Isa al-Thaqafi, Ibn Hurmuz, Zayd ibn Ali and an Asim transmission through Abu Bakr and Harun. Qurtubi compares the parallel vowel variants of ʿusr and yusr. Qurtubi explains the damma as vowel-following."}, {"id": "103:2/q04/p3", "position": "An explanatory recitation adds that humanity remains in loss until time's end, sometimes also adding time's calamities.", "reasons": "Ali is cited by Tabari, Thalabi, Mawardi, Qurtubi and Elmalili; Thalabi also attributes the time's-end addition to Ibn Masud, and Tabari reports Qatada. The variants differ over whether calamities are included. Qurtubi rejects this as canonical Qur'an. Ibn Atiyya also reports Ali's shorter opening variant, 'By the vicissitudes of time, mankind is in loss.' Durr relates Ibn Masud's time's-end wording through Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim, and Abd Allah ibn Utba; Abd Allah ibn Utba affirms it against Bishr ibn Marwan's accusation of disbelief."}, {"id": "103:2/q04/p4", "position": "Ibn Masud's codex says God created humanity in loss.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya records the wording of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masud's codex."}]}
{"id": "103:2/q05", "question": "What is the force of inna and la-fī?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase depicts an eventual outcome or a continuing condition.", "positions": [{"id": "103:2/q05/p1", "position": "Inna emphasizes the assertion and fī portrays the human as immersed and surrounded by loss.", "reasons": "Razi assigns emphasis to inna and describes loss encompassing a person from every side. Razi adds that the emphatic lam works with inna; Ibn ʿĀshūr says figurative containment is stronger than simply calling someone a loser."}, {"id": "103:2/q05/p2", "position": "La-fī can speak of an inevitable route toward future loss.", "reasons": "Razi compares 4:10, where eating orphans' property is expressed as fire already in bellies because that will be its outcome."}, {"id": "103:2/q05/p3", "position": "La-fī can speak of continual, inescapable loss in passing time.", "reasons": "For Razi each passing hour is capital rarely preserved: sin wastes it, permissible pursuits leave no enduring trace, and even worship may fall short of higher humility and knowledge."}]}
{"id": "103:2/q06", "question": "What does the indefinite khusr convey?", "turns_on": "Whether indefiniteness signals magnitude, a distinct or unrestricted category, or relative smallness.", "positions": [{"id": "103:2/q06/p1", "position": "It magnifies a loss whose full extent is known only to God.", "reasons": "Razi prefers this because sins oppose God and immense blessings; Baydawi, Bursevi and others also intensify the loss. Bint al-Shati cites Razi's awe explanation, but rejects treating intensity as its sole force. Ibn ʿĀshūr relates magnification to the threatening context of the oath."}, {"id": "103:2/q06/p2", "position": "It marks a distinctive kind or range of loss, beyond ordinary financial or social losses.", "reasons": "Bursevi, Alusi, Elmalili and Tabatabai mention a particular kind; Ibn Ashur adds multiple kinds and dramatic universality, comparing afterlife loss. Bint al-Shati understands it as open-ended and unrestricted rather than simple amplification. Alusi calls it a kind of loss unfamiliar to people; Ibn ʿĀshūr allows multiple kinds and comprehensiveness."}, {"id": "103:2/q06/p3", "position": "It can belittle human loss in comparison with Satan's.", "reasons": "Razi reports this consoling possibility: others are more disobedient, though he prefers magnification."}]}
{"id": "103:2/q07", "question": "What does khusr mean, and what is lost?", "turns_on": "Whether loss is read as a lexical diminution, unbelief, punishment, squandered life, spiritual deprivation, bodily decline or loss across both worlds.", "positions": [{"id": "103:2/q07/p1", "position": "Loss, ruin, diminishment, or destruction of one's capital.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda, Ibn Qutayba, Tabari, Suddi, Ibn Shajara, Akhfash and others give these overlapping lexical glosses; Ibn al-Jawzi says khusr and khusran are equivalent. Wahidi likens it to lost capital. Razi and Raghib note that loss may be predicated of a person or a transaction; Kashshaf compares the nominal forms. Bagawi and Ibn al-Jawzi identify the self as the greatest capital. Ibn Qutayba glosses loss as deficiency and says the excepted believers are not diminished. Ibn al-Jawzi says khusrān is conventionally a reduction of one's capital. Al-Damghani's sense list also includes decrease, without supplying an example in this extract. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats loss as the opposite of trading profit and compares an unprofitable trade in 2:16. Ibn Atiyya includes a bad condition among its senses."}, {"id": "103:2/q07/p2", "position": "Misguidance and disbelief that persist until death without faith.", "reasons": "Mujahid glosses loss as misguidance; Wahidi reports Muqatil's worldly explanation, and Razi links the particular-unbeliever interpretation to misguidance and belief as profit. Muqatil says Abu Lahab remains in error until Fire. Al-Damghani applies the sense 'misguidance' directly to humanity here and cites 4:119; Ibn al-Jawzi reports the same gloss from the exegetes, also with 4:119."}, {"id": "103:2/q07/p3", "position": "Punishment for sins, especially Fire and forfeited home, family or property in Paradise.", "reasons": "Farra, Mawardi and Qurtubi cite punishment, with Qurtubi comparing 65:9; Nahhas calls entry into Fire the greatest loss. Wahidi adds the forfeited Paradise station. Hasan adds void deeds; Jishumi sees lasting punishment as unsurpassable. Tabrisi and Qur'an 39:15 are used for loss of self and family at Judgment. Al-Damghani lists punishment as another sense of khusr, although this extract ends before its examples."}, {"id": "103:2/q07/p4", "position": "Evil or deprivation.", "reasons": "Zayd ibn Aslam gives evil in Mawardi; Ibn Zayd gives evil in Qurtubi, w

{"id": "103:2/q08", "question": "Why does ordinary human life tend toward loss?", "turns_on": "How finite life and human choices produce loss or enduring gain.", "positions": [{"id": "103:2/q08/p1", "position": "Life and time are finite capital; misuse or failure to earn lasting good spends them irretrievably.", "reasons": "Bagawi calls self and lifetime the greatest capital. Razi says sin, permissible activity and even incomplete worship miss enduring gain; Elmalili compares every breath to an entrusted loan and cites 25:62, 53:39 and 52:21. Poems about each passing day, his elegy and the image of death consuming life sharpen the point. Tabatabai calls earthly life a test (13:26; 21:35) in which belief and deeds determine the afterlife (53:39–41; 30:44; 41:46). Islahi stresses rapidly consumed life. Bint al-Shati's broad al-insan usage is distinguished from al-nas and jinn contexts. Baydawi and Alusi say people spend life in pursuits that yield no afterlife benefit; Alusi adds possible harm at resurrection. Biqai stresses attachment to the passing present."}, {"id": "103:2/q08/p2", "position": "Human desire, distraction and frailty draw people away from lasting good.", "reasons": "Sulami mentions neglect of God's rights, following desires and lack of fear. Razi says the afterlife's rewards are hidden whereas sensory appetites and anger draw people toward the visible world; Elmalili reports this. Biqai cites human injustice and ignorance (33:72) and notes that only a few are preserved from these defects. Qutb applies the loss to communities without righteous authority. Biqai describes loss as driven by whims, personal aims and delusion about what passes away; Ibn al-Zubayr connects innate injustice and ignorance in 33:72."}, {"id": "103:2/q08/p3", "position": "A person can turn life's expense into profit by using the present for faith, obedience and the afterlife.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan contrasts trading away the afterlife for this world with buying it through this world. Elmalili reports the Sufi call to be the child of the moment and distinguishes it from worldly pleasure seeking; a final righteous act may compensate past waste. He denies the poem's blaming of time, locating corruption in human conduct. Qutb stresses the enduring stakes. Kashshaf describes the righteous as buying the afterlife with this world and gaining happiness; Abu Hayyan says the reverse transaction is the greatest loss."}]}
{"id": "103:2/q09", "question": "Who escapes loss, and to what extent?", "turns_on": "Whether exemption requires all four traits and whether a believer's sinful or incomplete action still entails a degree of loss.", "positions": [{"id": "103:2/q09/p1", "position": "The complete exception requires faith, righteous deeds, and mutual counsel in truth and patience.", "reasons": "Muhammad ibn Kaʿb says belief alone is insufficient and lists the successive conditions. Muqatil says those who do these things remain in the Gardens; Elmalili calls the four complete faith; Qutb calls them the single successful path in every age and the basis of a community. Al-Shafiʿi and others regard the surah as sufficient guidance. Tabari and Hasan compare another connected exception with this one. Ibn Qutayba says those who believe, do good and counsel truth and patience are not diminished."}, {"id": "103:2/q09/p2", "position": "Believers who do righteous deeds are exempted from the loss.", "reasons": "Mujahid identifies the excepted believers; Muqatil and Thalabi also name belief and deeds. Razi says believers gain enduring happiness with their self and time. Ibn Ashur says good believers avoid loss when they do no opposite deed or repent; al-salihat includes commanded good and avoidance of sin. Islahi says deeds show faith has taken root, cites 4:136, and explains their outward, inward, worldly, religious, individual and collective scope through Farahi. Ibn Atiyya says believers' temporary hardship is forgiven beside lasting success; Ibrāhīm says their youthful deeds continue to be credited in decline."}, {"id": "103:2/q09/p3", "position": "Sinful believers incur a lesser, possibly temporary loss, though faith ultimately saves them.", "reasons": "Biqai distinguishes denial from losses proportionate to disobedience. Elmalili rejects the Murji'a claim that faith without action entails no loss; sinful believers whose evil outweighs good may experience Hell until cleansed. Ibn Ashur distinguishes eternal loss through denial from graded lesser losses and cites 11:114 on forgiveness of minor sins. Samarrai says mutual counsel prevents loss of further reward. Alusi says one outside the exception need not face eternal Fire: an unpardoned sinner may enter Fire, while a pardoned one may lose higher ranks. He calls other, unspecified replies offered by al-Maturidi strained."}, {"id": "103:2/q09/p4", "position": "Faith without action incurs no loss.", "reasons": "Elmalili attributes this to the Murji'a and explicitly rejects it in favor of graded loss for disobedient believers."}]}
{"id": "103:2/q10", "question": "How is the oath by time related to the human loss that follows?", "turns_on": "Whether the oath evokes life's finite capital, the late hour and reckoning, or time's warning events.", "positions": [{"id": "103:2/q10/p1", "position": "Time is the valuable, vanishing opportunity in which human gain or loss is determined.", "reasons": "Elmalili says time contains changes, wonders, blessing, harm and the chance to act; its passing consumes life unless used for faith and reform. He says the oath honors time rather than blaming it, and its senses of restraint and bestowal evoke both loss and gain. Kuranyolu similarly says God swears by precious time; Islahi relates it to responsibility for life's blessing. Baydawi says the oath indirectly denies that time causes loss; Alusi places responsibility on people amid time's blessings and opposites, while calling an identification of ʿasr with dahr unclear. Biqai associates ʿasr with time's essence and the extraction of essences."}, {"id": "103:2/q10/p2", "position": "Late afternoon evokes the closing human era or the end of life and the reckoning of what was earned.", "reasons": "Elmalili evokes creation late in the world's day, the era of Muhammad and the sorrow of returning without gain.
